title: Why Does Draft Beer Give Me a Headache? Pints, Taps, and Fixes
excerpt: Why draft beer gives you a headache: bigger pints and stronger craft beers, bar-night habits, what dirty tap lines really do, histamine and tyramine, and how to avoid it.
metaDescription: Why draft beer gives you a headache: bigger pints, stronger beers, dirty tap lines, histamine and tyramine. What really causes it and how to avoid it.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** most headaches from draft beer come from the same things that cause headaches from any beer, with a few twists that make them more likely at the bar. The biggest one is simple volume. A draft pint is usually bigger than a can, and draft menus lean toward stronger craft styles, so "two beers" on tap can easily be three or four standard drinks. On top of that you tend to drink faster at a bar, drink less water, and stay up later. Dirty tap lines get a lot of blame online, and they really can make beer taste off, but there is no good evidence that a poorly cleaned line is a common cause of headaches. Some people are also sensitive to histamine and tyramine, natural compounds found in beer that can trigger headaches in a minority of drinkers.

**The quick fixes:** count your pours in standard drinks rather than glasses, ask for a smaller pour or a lower-strength beer, drink a glass of water between rounds, and eat before and while you drink. If draft beer gives you a headache after just one glass, it is worth trying the same beer from a bottle or can on a different night. If the headache follows you, the beer itself (or alcohol) is the likely trigger, not the tap.

> **When to see a doctor.** Most drinking headaches are a nuisance, not an emergency. **Get emergency care (call 911 in the US) if** a headache is sudden and severe, like the worst headache of your life, or comes with confusion, a stiff neck, fever, weakness or numbness on one side, trouble speaking, vision loss, fainting, or repeated vomiting. Also get urgent help if you hit your head while drinking. **See a doctor soon if** you get headaches from even small amounts of alcohol, your headaches are getting more frequent or changing in pattern, you have flushing, hives, wheezing, or a racing heart after drinking, or you take an MAOI antidepressant (see the tyramine section below). If you have been drinking heavily every day and get headaches, shaking, and sweating when you stop, that can be alcohol withdrawal, and you should talk to a doctor before stopping on your own. This article is general information, not medical advice.

## Why Does Draft Beer Give Me a Headache? The Main Causes, Ranked

Here's a rough order of how likely each cause is for a typical social drinker. The top items explain the large majority of bar-night headaches. The bottom items are real but less common.

| Cause | How common | What points to it |
|---|---|---|
| More alcohol than you think (pint size and strength) | Very common | Headache the next morning, scales with how many rounds you had |
| Dehydration and poor sleep | Very common | Thirst, dry mouth, worse after a late night |
| Drinking fast on an empty stomach | Common | Headache comes on during or soon after drinking |
| Histamine or tyramine sensitivity | Less common | Headache, flushing, or stuffy nose after one or two drinks |
| Migraine triggered by alcohol | Less common | You already get migraines, and they start within hours of drinking |
| Off-tasting beer from dirty tap lines | Uncommon as a headache cause | The beer tastes buttery, sour, or stale |

Most of the time, the answer is in the top two rows. That's not as exciting as a dirty tap line, but it's the explanation with the best evidence and the easiest fix.

## Pint Size: The Draft Beer Headache Nobody Counts

The most overlooked cause of draft beer headaches is that a "beer" on tap is often much more than one drink.

In the US, one **standard drink** contains about 14 grams of pure alcohol. That's roughly the amount in a 12-ounce beer at 5% alcohol by volume (ABV), according to the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA). Draft beer breaks that math in two ways.

**The glass is bigger.** A US "pint" is 16 ounces, a third more than a standard can. A British imperial pint is about 20 ounces. Some bars pour into 20- or 23-ounce glasses and still call it a pint. Others use "cheater" pint glasses that hold closer to 14 ounces. You often don't know which you're getting.

**The beer is stronger.** Draft lists at bars and taprooms tend to feature craft styles. A lot of IPAs sit at 6% to 7.5% ABV, double IPAs often run 8% to 10%, and imperial stouts can go higher. A light lager might be 4% to 4.5%.

Here's what that looks like in standard drinks (approximate, using 0.6 ounces of pure alcohol per standard drink):

| What you ordered | Approximate standard drinks |
|---|---|
| 12 oz can, 5% lager | 1.0 |
| 16 oz pint, 5% lager | 1.3 |
| 16 oz pint, 7% IPA | 1.9 |
| 20 oz imperial pint, 5% lager | 1.7 |
| 20 oz pint, 7% IPA | 2.3 |
| 16 oz pint, 9% double IPA | 2.4 |

So three 16-ounce IPAs at 7% is close to six standard drinks. Most people would describe that night as "only three beers." The next-morning headache is behaving exactly as it should for six drinks.

If you want a quick way to check a specific pour, our [beer hangover guide](/never-hungover/beer-hangover) goes into the beer side of this in more detail. For the headache specifically, including histamine and dehydration, see our guide to [beer headaches](/never-hungover/beer-headache).

### Why this hits harder at the bar

Bigger, stronger pours often come with a faster pace. Rounds get bought for the table, conversation moves fast, and a pint glass empties quicker than you'd expect. Your liver clears alcohol at a fairly steady rate, often quoted as roughly one standard drink per hour, though it varies a lot between people. When you drink faster than that, your blood alcohol rises and stays high longer, and the headache the next day tends to be worse.

## Dehydration, Late Nights, and the Bar Environment

Alcohol suppresses a hormone called vasopressin (also known as antidiuretic hormone), which normally tells your kidneys to hold on to water. With less of it, you urinate more than you drink. Beer has a lot of water in it, which softens this effect compared with spirits, but it doesn't cancel it, especially with stronger beers. For more on how this works and how much it really matters, see our explainer on [whether alcohol dehydrates you](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-dehydrate-you).

The research on hangovers suggests dehydration is a contributor rather than the whole story. Studies have not found a tight link between how dehydrated people are and how bad their hangover feels. Still, being short on fluids can make a headache worse, and it's one of the easiest things to fix.

The bar itself adds a few more pressures:

- **Late nights.** Alcohol already makes the second half of your sleep lighter and more broken. Getting home at 1 a.m. on top of that leaves you short on sleep, and poor sleep is a well-known headache trigger on its own.
- **Noise and crowds.** Loud music and shouting over it for hours can leave you tense and tired, which some people feel as a tension-type headache.
- **Skipping food.** It's easy to drink two pints before the food arrives, or skip dinner entirely. Food in your stomach slows how fast alcohol reaches your blood.
- **Salty bar snacks and little water.** Pretzels and chips without a glass of water don't help.

None of these are unique to draft beer, but they cluster around it, because draft beer is mostly something you drink while out.

## Dirty Tap Lines: Real Problem, Weak Link to Headaches

This is the cause most people find online, so it deserves a careful look.

### What actually happens in a dirty line

Draft beer travels from a keg through plastic tubing (the "line") to the faucet. Over time, the inside of that tubing builds up yeast, bacteria, mineral deposits called beer stone, and a sticky film. The Brewers Association's *Draught Beer Quality Manual*, the main industry reference in the US, recommends cleaning lines with a chemical solution at least every two weeks, plus periodic acid cleaning to remove mineral buildup. Not every bar keeps to that schedule.

When lines go uncleaned, the beer picks up off flavors. Common ones include:

- **Buttery or butterscotch flavor**, from a compound called diacetyl, often produced by bacteria growing in the lines
- **Sour or vinegar notes**, from bacteria that spoil beer
- **Stale, musty, or flat taste**
- **Cloudiness** in a beer that should be clear

### Does it cause headaches?

There is no good evidence that dirty tap lines are a common cause of headaches. The bacteria that grow in beer lines are mostly spoilage organisms. They ruin the flavor, but beer's alcohol, acidity, and hops make it a hostile place for the germs that typically cause food poisoning. We are not aware of solid research tying poorly maintained draft systems to headaches in drinkers.

There are a couple of plausible but unproven links worth knowing about:

- **Biogenic amines.** Some of the bacteria that spoil beer can produce histamine and tyramine. In theory, a badly contaminated line could raise the levels in the glass. Whether that happens often enough to matter in real bars hasn't been well studied.
- **Cleaning residue.** Line cleaner is a strong alkaline chemical. If a line isn't rinsed properly after cleaning, the first pours can taste soapy or chemical. A bar with good practice flushes the line with water and then beer before serving. If your beer tastes like soap, send it back.

The practical takeaway: **trust your tongue.** If a draft beer tastes buttery when it shouldn't, sour when it isn't a sour beer, or soapy, send it back or switch to a bottle. That's good advice for flavor reasons alone. But if the beer tastes fine and you still get a headache, the tap line is probably not your problem.

## Histamine and Tyramine: When One Draft Beer Is Enough

If you get a headache after just one or two glasses, and especially if it comes with a flushed face, stuffy nose, or itchy skin, you may be reacting to compounds in the beer rather than the amount of alcohol.

### Histamine

Histamine is a natural compound made during fermentation. Beer, and especially wine, contain small amounts. Most people break it down in their gut with an enzyme called diamine oxidase (DAO). People with lower DAO activity, sometimes described as histamine intolerance, can react to histamine-rich foods and drinks with headaches, flushing, a runny nose, or hives. Alcohol itself may also interfere with how well DAO works, which can make the reaction worse. Our guide to [histamine intolerance and alcohol](/never-hungover/histamine-intolerance-and-alcohol) covers this in more depth.

Histamine levels vary a lot between beers. Researchers have generally found higher levels of biogenic amines in some sour and spontaneously fermented beers, which use wild yeasts and bacteria on purpose, than in standard lagers. If you notice your headaches show up with sours or certain craft styles, that's a useful clue.

### Tyramine

Tyramine is another amine found in aged, fermented, and some tap beers. In most people it does nothing noticeable. In some people prone to migraine, it's a suspected trigger, though the evidence on that is mixed.

**There is one group for whom tyramine is a real safety issue:** people taking MAOI antidepressants (such as phenelzine or tranylcypromine) or certain other medicines in the same class. MAOIs block the enzyme that breaks down tyramine, and a large tyramine dose can cause a dangerous spike in blood pressure with a pounding headache. MAOI diet guidance has long singled out **tap and unpasteurized beers** as a higher-risk choice than bottled or canned beer. If you take an MAOI, talk to your doctor or pharmacist about which beers, if any, are safe for you. A severe, pounding headache with a racing heart, chest pain, or a stiff neck while on an MAOI is an emergency.

### Why draft beer might differ from bottled

Some draft beer, especially from smaller craft breweries, is unpasteurized and may be unfiltered. That's partly why it can taste fresher. Unpasteurized beer can contain live yeast and may change a little over time in the keg. It's possible that some unpasteurized draft beers carry more amines than a pasteurized bottle of the same beer, which is the reason behind the MAOI warning. For people without a specific sensitivity, there's no good evidence that this difference causes headaches.

## Draft Beer vs. Bottled Beer: Why One Feels Worse

Plenty of people say draft beer gives them a headache but the same beer from a can doesn't. A few explanations fit that pattern, roughly from most to least likely:

1. **Different amounts.** A pint on tap is bigger than a 12-ounce bottle. Over a night, the difference adds up.
2. **Different settings.** You usually drink bottled beer at home, slower, with food, and you go to bed on time. Draft beer usually comes with a bar night.
3. **Different beers.** The draft list is often stronger and more varied than what's in your fridge. You might be trying a 9% stout on tap that you'd never buy in a six-pack.
4. **Unpasteurized or unfiltered beer.** For people sensitive to histamine or tyramine, this could matter.
5. **Spoiled beer from a bad line.** Possible, but usually your taste buds will warn you.

**A simple test:** order the same beer you drink at home, in a measured amount, on a night when you eat a proper meal and drink water alongside it. If the headache disappears, the cause was the amount, pace, or setting. If it still shows up after a single glass, a sensitivity to something in the beer (or to alcohol itself) is more likely. Keep a short note on your phone of what you drank, how much, and how you felt. Patterns show up faster than you'd think.

## Carbonation and Nitro Pours

Draft beer is served under gas pressure, usually carbon dioxide, and some stouts are poured "on nitro" with a nitrogen blend for a creamy head. Some research suggests carbonated drinks may speed up how quickly alcohol is absorbed, at least for mixed drinks, though the findings aren't entirely consistent. Faster absorption means a quicker rise in blood alcohol, which may make some people feel effects sooner.

Being bloated from carbonation is uncomfortable, but there's no good evidence that carbonation alone causes headaches. Nitro pours are actually less fizzy than standard draft beer. If you suspect bubbles bother you, a nitro stout or a less carbonated cask ale is an easy experiment.

## Migraine and Alcohol

If you already get migraines, alcohol is one of the most commonly reported triggers. Many people with migraine say red wine is the worst offender, but beer and spirits are reported as triggers too. An alcohol-triggered migraine can start within a few hours of drinking, rather than the next morning, and often comes with sensitivity to light and sound, nausea, or a one-sided throbbing headache.

If that sounds like you, our guide to [migraines after drinking](/never-hungover/migraine-after-drinking) covers triggers, timing, and what to discuss with your doctor. People with migraine sometimes find they tolerate one specific drink better than others, and keeping a headache diary is the best way to find out.

## Gluten and Other Ingredients

People sometimes wonder whether gluten causes beer headaches. For most people, it doesn't. For people with celiac disease or non-celiac gluten sensitivity, headaches can be one of several symptoms after eating or drinking gluten, along with digestive symptoms and fatigue. Most beers are made from barley and contain gluten, including draft beers. If you suspect gluten, look at our guide to [gluten-free alcohol](/never-hungover/gluten-free-alcohol) and talk to your doctor about testing before cutting it out, since testing works best while you're still eating gluten.

Some craft draft beers also include fruit, spices, lactose (in milkshake IPAs and some stouts), or added flavorings. If your headaches only show up with certain specialty beers, an ingredient could be the link.

## How to Avoid a Draft Beer Headache

These steps are listed from most to least useful for a typical night out.

1. **Count in standard drinks, not glasses.** Check the ABV on the menu and the size of the pour. A 16-ounce 7% IPA is almost two drinks.
2. **Order smaller pours.** Many bars offer 10- or 12-ounce pours, half pints, or tasting flights. You still get to try the beer.
3. **Pick lower-ABV beers.** A session IPA, pilsner, or light lager in the 4% to 5% range cuts your alcohol intake a lot over a full night.
4. **Alternate with water.** One glass of water per beer slows your pace and helps with fluids. Ask the bartender for a water at the same time as your round.
5. **Eat before and during.** A real meal before you start, and something to eat while you drink, slows how fast alcohol reaches your blood.
6. **Slow your pace.** Aim for no more than about one standard drink an hour, keeping in mind a big IPA might be two.
7. **Send back beer that tastes wrong.** Buttery, sour, soapy, or stale flavors in a beer that shouldn't have them are worth flagging.
8. **Go home a bit earlier.** Sleep is underrated as a headache preventer.
9. **Test your sensitivity.** If one glass triggers a headache, try the same beer from a can at home. If it still happens, see the histamine and doctor sections above.

For a broader set of habits with decent evidence behind them, our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) is a good next read.

## What to Do If You Already Have the Headache

- **Drink water,** and consider an electrolyte drink if you're also queasy or have been sweating.
- **Eat something simple,** such as toast, bananas, eggs, or soup.
- **Rest in a dark, quiet room** if light and noise are bothering you.
- **Be careful with painkillers.** Ibuprofen, naproxen, and aspirin can irritate a stomach that's already irritated by alcohol, so take them with food and stick to the label. Acetaminophen (Tylenol) is processed by the liver, and its label warns people who have 3 or more drinks a day to ask a doctor first. Don't take any painkiller "just in case" before bed. Our guide to [the alcohol headache and how to relieve it](/never-hungover/alcohol-headache-why-it-happens-how-to-prevent-2025) covers the options in more detail.
- **Caffeine,** in moderation, helps some people with headache, but it can also upset your stomach and add to dehydration if you overdo it.
- **Skip the "hair of the dog."** Another beer may delay the headache, but it only postpones the recovery.

If you get a headache after only a single glass, see our page on [headaches after one drink](/never-hungover/headache-after-one-drink), which looks at the causes when the amount clearly isn't the problem.

## Where DHM Fits (and Where It Doesn't)

Some people take dihydromyricetin (DHM), a compound from the Japanese raisin tree, before or after a night out. Here's the honest picture: most of the research on DHM and alcohol comes from animal and lab studies, which suggest it may affect how the body handles alcohol and its by-products. Human evidence is limited. There is no good evidence that DHM prevents draft beer headaches specifically, and it won't help with histamine sensitivity, migraine, or a sensitivity to gluten. It also doesn't change how much alcohol is in your pint, so it's no substitute for counting drinks.

If you'd like to try it alongside the habits above, a straightforward, well-reviewed option is [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains typical amounts and timing, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. If you take prescription medicine, check with your pharmacist before adding any supplement.

## The Bottom Line

- The most common reason draft beer gives you a headache is that a draft "beer" is often well over one standard drink. Bigger glasses and stronger craft styles add up fast.
- Bar nights also bring faster drinking, less water, less food, and less sleep, all of which make headaches more likely.
- Dirty tap lines can make beer taste buttery, sour, or soapy, but there is no good evidence they are a common cause of headaches. Send back beer that tastes wrong.
- If you get a headache after one glass, especially with flushing or a stuffy nose, histamine or tyramine sensitivity, migraine, or a reaction to an ingredient could be the reason.
- If you take an MAOI antidepressant, ask your doctor about tap and unpasteurized beers, which can be high in tyramine.
- Get emergency care for a sudden, severe headache or one with confusion, stiff neck, weakness, or vision changes.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Why does draft beer give me a headache but bottled beer doesn't?**

The most likely reasons are amount and setting. A draft pint is usually 16 to 20 ounces, compared with a 12-ounce bottle, and draft lists often feature stronger beers. Draft beer also tends to come with bar nights, which mean faster drinking, less water, and less sleep. Less often, some people may react to unpasteurized or unfiltered draft beer, which can contain more histamine or tyramine. Try the same beer in a measured amount at home to see which explanation fits you.

**Can dirty tap lines give you a headache?**

There is no good evidence that dirty tap lines are a common cause of headaches. Uncleaned lines grow bacteria and yeast that make beer taste buttery, sour, or stale, and the industry's Draught Beer Quality Manual recommends cleaning lines at least every two weeks. Spoiled beer is unpleasant, and it's possible some contamination raises amine levels, but that hasn't been well studied. If a beer tastes off, send it back.

**How many standard drinks are in a pint of draft beer?**

It depends on the glass and the beer. A 16-ounce US pint of 5% lager is about 1.3 standard drinks. A 16-ounce pint of 7% IPA is about 1.9, and a 20-ounce imperial pint of the same IPA is about 2.3. A US standard drink is about 14 grams of alcohol, roughly a 12-ounce beer at 5%.

**Why do I get a headache after just one draft beer?**

If one glass reliably triggers a headache, the amount of alcohol probably isn't the main cause. Possible reasons include sensitivity to histamine or tyramine in the beer, migraine triggered by alcohol, sensitivity to an ingredient such as gluten, or drinking quickly on an empty stomach. If it keeps happening, or comes with flushing, hives, wheezing, or a racing heart, talk to a doctor.

**Is draft beer higher in histamine or tyramine?**

It can be, depending on the beer. Unpasteurized beers, which include many draft craft beers, can contain more tyramine, which is why MAOI diet guidance has long flagged tap and unpasteurized beers. Sour and wild-fermented beers often have higher levels of biogenic amines than standard lagers. For most people these amounts cause no problems, but people with histamine intolerance or who take MAOIs should be more careful.

**When is a headache after drinking beer an emergency?**

Get emergency care if the headache is sudden and severe, or comes with confusion, a stiff neck, fever, weakness or numbness, trouble speaking, vision loss, fainting, or repeated vomiting. Also get help after any head injury while drinking. If you take an MAOI and get a pounding headache with a racing heart or chest pain after drinking tap beer, call 911.

**Does DHM stop beer headaches?**

There is no good evidence that DHM prevents beer headaches specifically. Most DHM research comes from animal and lab studies, with limited human data. It won't help with histamine sensitivity, migraine, or gluten reactions, and it doesn't reduce the alcohol in your glass. Counting standard drinks, drinking water, and eating are the most reliable steps.
